text: Today, most scientists agree that the non-bird dinosaurs died out about 66 million years ago, after an [[asteroid|asteroid]] about 10 kilometres wide slammed into what is now Mexico. But that idea only became popular after 1980. Before then, people suggested dozens of other explanations, some sensible, some very strange.

Over the years, dinosaurs were blamed on disease, cold weather, egg-eating [[mammal|mammals]], caterpillars, poisonous plants, exploding stars and even their own bodies wearing out as a group. A few of these ideas had real evidence behind them. Many did not. One old rival, giant volcanic eruptions in India, is still taken seriously as a partner to the asteroid.

st.prompt: What clue first made scientists suspect a rock from space?

options.t: A thin layer of clay full of a metal that is rare on Earth but common in asteroids
A dinosaur skeleton with a hole in its skull

st.reveal: In 1980, the Alvarez team found a layer of clay rich in iridium at the exact level in the rocks where dinosaurs disappear. Iridium is rare in Earth's crust but more common in asteroids. The same layer was later found around the world.

n.certNote: Nearly all scientists agree a giant asteroid impact 66 million years ago was the main cause. They still debate how much India's huge Deccan volcanic eruptions added, and whether some dinosaur groups were already in decline.

myth: The dinosaurs died out because they were too big and slow to survive.

Dinosaurs ruled for more than 160 million years and came in every size, including small, fast ones. Many small species died too, and one group of small, feathered dinosaurs survived as birds. Size alone doesn't explain it.

1980, by Luis and Walter Alvarez and colleagues

sec.t:
Early in the 1900s, some scientists thought dinosaurs simply grew too big, too spiky or too odd, as if the whole group had become old and tired. This "racial old age" idea has been dropped. There is no sign that dinosaurs were weakening as a group.

Others thought small mammals ate too many dinosaur eggs. But mammals and dinosaurs had lived side by side for over 100 million years, so why would that suddenly cause a disaster? Some suggested that new flowering plants poisoned plant-eaters, or that swarms of caterpillars ate all the leaves. Flowering plants, though, had already been around for tens of millions of years.

In 1980, physicist Luis Alvarez and his son Walter, a [[geologist|geologist]], published a bold idea. Walter had studied a thin layer of clay in Italy that marks the exact end of the dinosaur age. It was full of [[@iridium-evidence|iridium]], a metal rare on Earth but common in asteroids. The team argued that a huge space rock had hit Earth.

Many experts were doubtful. Then, in 1991, scientists confirmed a buried [[crater|crater]] about 180 kilometres across at Chicxulub, on Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula. It was the right age. Tiny glass beads, shocked quartz and [[tsunami|tsunami]] deposits around the Gulf of Mexico fitted the story. Most scientists were convinced.

At around the same time, enormous eruptions were pouring out lava in western India. Over hundreds of thousands of years, they built the Deccan Traps, layers of rock that can be more than 2 kilometres thick. You can see their steps in the hills around Mumbai, Pune and Mahabaleshwar, and across much of the [[@deccan|Deccan Plateau]].

These eruptions pumped gases into the air that could have changed the climate. Some scientists think they weakened life before the asteroid struck. Others think their effect was small. The debate continues, and new dating of the lava layers keeps adding evidence.

Out of all these ideas, only the ones backed by evidence in the rocks survived. That is how science is meant to work: you suggest an idea, then hunt for clues that could prove it wrong.

The asteroid did not kill every dinosaur. Small feathered ones lived on, and their descendants are the [[@birds-dinosaurs|birds]] outside your window. Small mammals, turtles, crocodiles and frogs survived too, and the world they inherited became ours.

text: Sound doesn't fossilise. So scientists study dinosaurs' closest living relatives: birds and crocodiles.
Both can make deep, closed-mouth booming sounds. Dinosaurs probably could too. The sound may have been more like a deep rumble you feel in your chest than a movie roar.

The duck-billed Parasaurolophus had a hollow crest. Models of it make a low, trumpet-like hoot. Some dinosaurs may also have hissed, honked or clattered their beaks, but we can't hear any of it directly.

st.prompt: What sound do you think a big dinosaur made?
st.reveal: Many scientists think big dinosaurs boomed or cooed with closed mouths, like crocodiles and some birds do, a deep sound you'd feel in your chest. We can't know for sure, because sounds don't fossilise.
st.nudge: That's what the movies show! But their closest living relatives don't roar.

n.certNote: Sounds don't fossilise, so every idea about dinosaur voices comes from skull shapes and from their living relatives. Scientists agree on the clues but not on exactly what dinosaurs sounded like.

d.try: Hum a low note with your mouth closed, then put a hand on your chest and throat. You can feel the buzz. Now try with a cardboard tube held to your lips and hum again. A longer tube makes a deeper sound, which is how Parasaurolophus's long crest may have worked.
myth: Dinosaurs roared like lions with their mouths wide open.
There is no evidence for that. Their closest relatives, birds and crocodiles, often call with their mouths closed, making booms, hisses and coos. Many scientists think big dinosaurs did the same.
facts: Parasaurolophus, with tubes inside its crest

sec.t:
The roar of the T. rex in the 1993 film Jurassic Park was made by sound designers, who mixed recordings of real animals, including a baby elephant, a tiger and an alligator. It sounds terrifying, which was the point. It was never meant to be scientific.

Lions and tigers roar with their mouths open, pushing air through a voice box in the throat. [[mammal|Mammals]] have a different kind of voice box from birds, and dinosaurs were not mammals. So a lion's roar is not a good guide.

Parasaurolophus, a plant-eater that lived about 76 million years ago in North America, had a long, curved crest sweeping back from its head. Inside were tubes connected to its nose, looping up and back down. In 1981, a scientist argued that the crest worked like a wind instrument.

In the 1990s, researchers scanned a crest and built a [[@computers-how|computer model]] of the air passages. Blowing air through the model gave a low, resonant hoot. Different shapes of crest would make different notes. Males, females and youngsters may have sounded quite different. Young Parasaurolophus had much smaller crests, so their [[@animal-communication|calls]] would have been higher, the way a small flute sounds higher than a big one. Its relatives, like Corythosaurus with its helmet-shaped crest, had different tube shapes and probably made different calls.

Birds sing with an organ called a [[syrinx|syrinx]], deep in the chest where the windpipe splits. That is how some [[@birds-sing|songbirds]] can sing two notes at once. The oldest syrinx known comes from a bird called Vegavis, found in Antarctica and about 67 million years old.

In 2023, scientists described the [[fossil|fossil]] voice box of Pinacosaurus, an armoured dinosaur from Mongolia. It looked more like a bird's than a crocodile's. That hints that some dinosaurs could change their calls in bird-like ways, though not necessarily sing.

Big animals can make very low sounds that travel far. [[@elephants-talk|Elephants]] rumble to each other across several kilometres with sounds partly below what human ears can catch, called [[infrasound|infrasound]]. Giant dinosaurs had big bodies and long airways, so some may have done the same. If so, a herd of [[sauropod|sauropods]] might have been talking all around you and you would have felt it more than heard it.

text: The real Velociraptor was a small, fast, feathered hunter from the Gobi Desert in [[@mongolia|Mongolia]]. It lived about 75 million years ago. A grown one was about 2 m long, but most of that was tail. It weighed about as much as a large dog.

It had a curved killing claw on each foot, sharp teeth and long arms with feathers. If you saw one today, you might first think it was a strange, toothy bird. That would not be a silly mistake, because Velociraptor was a close cousin of [[@birds-dinosaurs|birds]].

st.prompt: How tall was a real Velociraptor at the hip?

options.t: About as high as your knee
About as tall as a grown-up

st.reveal: A grown Velociraptor stood about half a metre tall at the hip. It was about 2 m long, but much of that was a stiff tail. The big film raptors were based on a larger cousin called Deinonychus.

src: American Museum of Natural History, Central Asiatic Expeditions and Velociraptor fossils.
Turner A.H., Makovicky P.J. and Norell M.A. (2007) Feather quill knobs in the dinosaur Velociraptor. Science 317.
n.certNote: Its size, feathers and claws are known from good fossils. How it hunted, and whether it ever hunted in groups, is still a guess.

myth: Velociraptor was a tall, scaly hunter that could open doors.
The real animal was about the size of a turkey and was covered in feathers. The film monsters were made bigger on purpose, and there is no sign that any dinosaur opened doors.

sec.t:
The first Velociraptor skull was dug up in 1923 at a place called the Flaming Cliffs, in Mongolia. The team came from the American Museum of Natural History in New York. They had gone to the Gobi hunting for early humans, and found dinosaurs and nests of eggs instead.

The name, given in 1924, means "swift thief". Back then, the Gobi was a dry land of sand dunes and short-lived streams. Sudden sandstorms and collapsing dunes buried animals quickly, which is why its [[fossil|fossils]] are so well kept.

The most famous part of Velociraptor is the big curved claw on the second toe of each foot. Raptor footprints show only two toes touching the ground, so the claw was held up while walking, like a folded penknife. That kept its tip sharp.

Its skull was long and low, about as long as your forearm, with dozens of small teeth edged like a steak knife. The tail was stiffened by thin bony rods, so it worked like a balancing pole when the animal turned fast.

Some scientists think raptors used the foot claws to pin small prey down while they ate, the way a hawk or eagle does today. Velociraptor also took easy meals. One skeleton found in Mongolia has a piece of flying [[reptile|reptile]] bone in its belly. That reptile was probably too big for a Velociraptor to catch, so it may have been feeding on a body it found.

For years, artists drew Velociraptor with scales. Then, in 2007, scientists looked closely at a Velociraptor forearm bone. They found a row of small bumps called quill knobs. In living birds, these are where strong wing feathers attach to the bone.

So Velociraptor had real, long [[@feathers|feathers]] on its arms. It could not fly. It was far too heavy for its arm size. The feathers may have helped it show off, keep eggs warm, or balance while it pinned down prey.

The raptors in the 1993 film Jurassic Park were about as tall as the actors. The [[@hollywood|film makers]] chose the name Velociraptor because it sounded better. Their animals were really closer in size to Deinonychus, a larger relative from North America. When the film was made, scientists had not yet found the quill knobs either.

Films about pack-hunting raptors also go further than the evidence. Some raptor footprints in China show several animals walking side by side. Nobody has proof that Velociraptor itself hunted in teams, so that part remains an open question.

text: Pangaea was a supercontinent: a single giant landmass that held almost all of Earth's land. It came together roughly 335 to 300 million years ago and stayed in one piece for over a hundred million years. A single vast ocean, called Panthalassa, surrounded it.

Then, roughly 200 to 175 million years ago, Pangaea began to crack apart. The pieces slowly moved away from each other and became the continents on today's map. They are still moving now, a few centimetres a year.
The name comes from Greek words meaning "all land". It was used by Alfred Wegener, the scientist best known for arguing that the [[@continental-drift|continents drift]].

st.prompt: Pangaea was one giant piece of land. What was the middle of it probably like?
st.reveal: Rain usually comes from moist air blowing in off the sea. The heart of Pangaea was thousands of kilometres from any coast, so much of it was hot and dry, with deserts far bigger than any today.

src: Encyclopaedia Britannica, "Pangea".
Natural History Museum, London, plate tectonics and the history of the continents.
n.certNote: Geologists agree that Pangaea existed. Its exact dates vary by tens of millions of years between sources, and ideas about the next supercontinent are educated guesses.

myth: Pangaea was the first and only supercontinent.
Earth's continents have joined and split several times. An older supercontinent called Rodinia came together about a billion years ago, long before Pangaea.

sec.t:
Pangaea was home to some of the biggest moments in the history of life. About 252 million years ago, giant volcanic eruptions in what is now Siberia set off the [[@great-dying|Great Dying]], which wiped out most [[species|species]] in the sea and many on land.

Life recovered, and about 230 million years ago the first dinosaurs appeared. With one connected landmass, animals could spread almost everywhere. That is why [[fossil|fossils]] of closely related early dinosaurs and [[reptile|reptiles]] turn up on continents that are now oceans apart.

One of the best examples is Lystrosaurus, a stocky, pig-sized plant-eater with two short tusks. It survived the Great Dying and became one of the most common land animals for a while afterwards. Its bones have been dug up in South Africa, in India's Damodar valley, in China and even in Antarctica. An animal that size could never have swum between those places. It simply walked across one continent, long before the oceans opened between them.

Pangaea did not split all at once. First, a long crack opened between North America and Africa. Sea water flooded in, and the Atlantic Ocean was born. Pangaea split into a northern half, Laurasia, and a southern half, [[gondwana|Gondwana]].

Gondwana then broke into pieces too. India pulled away from Africa, then from Madagascar, and [[@india-drift|raced north]] at speeds of up to about 15 cm a year, which is fast for a continent. Around 50 million years ago it crashed into Asia and pushed up the [[@himalaya-form|Himalayas]]. Some of India's dinosaurs, like those found in Gujarat and Madhya Pradesh, lived on this island continent during its long voyage.

Supercontinents seem to come and go in a long cycle. Before Pangaea there was Rodinia, about a billion years ago, and perhaps others even earlier.

Many [[geologist|geologists]] think the continents will join again in about 200 to 300 million years. They disagree about how. Some models close the Atlantic, some close the Pacific, and some push everything together around the North Pole. These future maps have names like Pangaea Proxima and Amasia, and nobody will be around to check which one is right.

text: A battery is a little chemical factory in a can. Inside are two different materials, one at each end, called electrodes. Between them is a substance called an [[electrolyte|electrolyte]], often a paste or liquid, which lets electrically charged [[atom|atoms]] drift through but blocks [[electron|electrons]], the tiny charged particles that make electric current.

The two electrode materials "want" to react with each other, but they can't, because electrons can't cross the electrolyte. When you connect a wire from one end to the other, through a torch bulb or a toy motor, you give the electrons a path. They rush out of one end, through the wire, doing work on the way, and into the other end. The reaction keeps running until the chemicals are used up, and then the battery is flat.

st.prompt: What actually moves through the wire when a battery lights a torch bulb?

options.t: The chemicals from inside the battery

st.reveal: The chemicals stay inside the battery. Their reaction pushes electrons out of one end, through the wire and the bulb, and back into the other end. The flow of electrons is the electric current.

d.try: Go on a battery hunt at home with an adult. Look at the labels on remote controls, clocks, toys and old phones, and write down each battery's voltage and size. Which gives the most volts? Never open, puncture or burn a battery, and give old ones to an e-waste collection point instead of the bin.
myth: A battery stores electricity inside it, like a tank.

A battery stores chemical energy. Electricity is made only when you connect it in a circuit and the chemicals start reacting. A recharged battery has had those reactions pushed backwards by a charger.

sec.h: Frog legs and a pile of coins

sec.t:
Some reactions can be pushed backwards. When you plug in a phone, [[@chargers|the charger]] forces electrons back the wrong way, rebuilding the original chemicals. Then the battery is ready to run again.

Car batteries have done this for over a century using lead plates in [[acid|acid]]. Phones and laptops use lithium-ion batteries, which pack much more energy into a small, light space. In 2019, three scientists shared the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for developing them: John Goodenough of the USA, Stanley Whittingham, born in the UK, and Akira Yoshino of Japan. Goodenough was 97, the oldest person ever to win a Nobel Prize.

An AA cell gives 1.5 volts. Put several in a row and their pushes add up, which is why a torch might take two or three. An [[@electric-cars|electric car]] carries thousands of small lithium cells, linked together into one large pack under the floor that can weigh as much as a small cow.

Power companies now build giant batteries the size of warehouses. They store electricity from [[@solar-panels|solar panels]] during sunny afternoons and release it after dark. In India, both electric scooters and these large storage batteries are growing fast.

Batteries hold a lot of energy, so they need respect. A damaged or badly made lithium-ion battery can overheat and catch fire. Never puncture, crush or heat one, and let an adult deal with any battery that is swollen or leaking.

Old batteries contain metals that can poison soil and water, but also useful materials that can be recovered. Many shops and towns in India and the USA collect them for [[@recycling|recycling]]. A used AA cell has given up its energy, but its zinc and manganese can still be turned into something new.

text: When a ball spins, it drags a thin layer of air around with it. On one side, the spinning surface moves *with* the oncoming air; on the other side, it moves *against* it. That makes the air flow unevenly, and the ball gets pushed sideways. This is called the **Magnus effect**.

A curveball spins with topspin, so the push is mostly downward. It dives as it reaches the batter. Pitchers can tilt the spin to make the ball break down and sideways at the same time. The spin itself is about 2,500 turns a minute, so the ball rotates around 15 to 20 times on its short trip to the plate.

st.prompt: A ball spinning with its top going forward will curve…
st.reveal: Topspin makes the air push the ball down, so it dips sharply. Backspin does the opposite and keeps the ball up longer.

src: Nathan A.M. (2008) The effect of spin on the flight of a baseball. American Journal of Physics 76.
Adair R.K. (2002) The Physics of Baseball, 3rd ed.

d.try: Throw a light plastic ball or a beach ball to a friend, first with no spin, then flicking your fingers down the front of the ball to give it topspin, then down the side for sidespin. Watch how each throw bends. Light balls curve much more, so the effect is easy to see.
myth: A good fastball really rises as it reaches the batter.
No pitch thrown overarm can rise against gravity at these speeds. A fastball has strong backspin, so it drops less than the batter expects. To the batter, that looks like it jumped upward.

sec.t:
The pitcher stands 18.4 m from home plate. A fast pitch reaches the batter in under half a second, so batters must decide whether to swing almost before the ball leaves the hand.

Here is the [[@speed-distance|speed]] maths. At 150 km/h, a ball travels about 42 metres every second. The pitcher lets go a little in front of the mound, so the ball covers about 17 metres, which takes roughly 0.4 seconds. A batter needs about a quarter of a second just to swing. That leaves only a [[@sport-science-reaction-time|split second]] to judge the pitch.

A curve that dips late is very hard to hit. Curveballs are slower, often around 120 to 130 km/h, and during their flight they can drop many centimetres more than a ball with no spin.

For years, some people argued that curveballs only looked as if they curved. In 1959, the American physicist Lyman Briggs tested spinning baseballs in a wind tunnel and measured the sideways push. Later, high-speed [[@cameras-how|cameras]] and radar tracked thousands of pitches. The ball really does curve, and its path can be predicted from its speed and spin.

Today every pitch in a top-level game is tracked by cameras and radar. Teams know the spin rate of every pitch a pitcher throws.

The strangest pitch of all is the knuckleball. The pitcher pushes it out with the fingertips so that it barely spins at all. With almost no spin, small changes in the air around the seams make it flutter and wobble unpredictably. Even the catcher often does not know where it will go.

Cricket spin bowlers use the same physics. A ball spinning sideways can *drift* in the air before it even bounces.

There is one big difference. In cricket, the ball usually bounces before reaching the batter, and the spin grips the pitch to change direction again. In baseball, the ball must reach the batter on the full, so all the movement happens in the air.

text: A javelin flies far for three reasons: it's thrown very fast, at the right angle, and its long, thin shape lets it glide a little. Top men release the spear at around 28 to 30 metres a second, roughly 100 km/h. To get that speed, they sprint up a runway, then slam on the brakes with their front leg. Their whole body's momentum then whips through the throwing arm, like the crack of a whip.

Once in the air, a javelin isn't just falling. It behaves a bit like a narrow [[@airplanes-fly|aeroplane wing]]. Air flowing past it gives it a little [[lift|lift]], keeping it up a little longer. Throwers have to get everything right: the speed, the angle of release and the angle of the tip.

st.prompt: To throw a ball as far as possible, you'd launch it at about 45 degrees. What angle do top javelin throwers use?
st.reveal: A javelin isn't a ball. It glides a little, like a narrow wing, and throwers release it from above head height. Both of these mean a flatter launch, often in the low to mid 30s of degrees, gives the longest throw.

d.try: Make paper darts and test launch angles. Throw the same dart five times each at a low angle, a medium angle and a high angle, keeping your throw equally strong. Measure each landing spot with a tape or your steps. Which angle wins? Then try moving a paperclip from the nose to the middle, and watch how its flight changes.
myth: The javelin flies like a stone, so only arm strength matters.
A javelin is shaped to glide. The angle it's released at, the angle of its tip and where its weight sits all change the distance. Technique matters as much as muscle.

sec.t:
The run-up is usually about 30 metres. In the last few strides, the thrower turns sideways and pulls the javelin back to full stretch. The final step is a hard block with the front leg, which stops the hips. Energy then travels upwards: hips, chest, shoulder, elbow, wrist and finally fingers, each moving faster than the last.

This chain is the same one cricket fast bowlers and baseball pitchers use. It puts huge strain on elbows and shoulders, which is why javelin throwers often fight injuries.

sec.h: The throw that changed the javelin
sec.t:
In 1984 Uwe Hohn of East Germany threw the old men's javelin 104.80 metres. It was too far for safety. Stadiums have a running track wrapped around the field, and javelins were starting to fly dangerously far. Old javelins also often landed flat, so judges argued about where they had hit.

In 1986 the rules changed. The new men's javelin had its balance point moved about 4 centimetres towards the front. Now the nose dips earlier, the javelin flies a shorter, steeper path, and it sticks into the ground tip first. Distances dropped sharply overnight. The women's javelin was redesigned in the same way in 1999. Hohn's 104.80 metres will stand for ever as the record for the old design.

On 7 August 2021, at the delayed Tokyo Olympics, [[@neeraj-chopra|Neeraj Chopra]] threw 87.58 metres to win gold. It was independent India's first Olympic gold in athletics. India's athletics federation now marks 7 August as National Javelin Day. Chopra also won the World Championships in 2023 and Olympic silver in Paris in 2024, where Pakistan's Arshad Nadeem won gold with an Olympic record of 92.97 metres. In May 2025, Chopra finally crossed 90 metres, with 90.23 metres in Doha.

People have thrown spears for hunting for hundreds of thousands of years. The ancient Greeks made javelin throwing part of the pentathlon at the [[@ancient-olympia|ancient Olympics]]. They wrapped a leather strap around the shaft and held its loop with their fingers. As the spear left the hand, the strap unwound and set it spinning, which kept it steady, like the spin on a rifle bullet.

And the strangest part? Changing the balance point of a javelin works just like moving a paperclip on a [[@paper-planes|paper plane]]: shift the weight forward and the nose dives sooner.

text: नील तब पड़ता है जब किसी टक्कर से त्वचा के नीचे की नन्ही खून की नलियाँ, जिन्हें [[capillary|केशिकाएँ]] कहते हैं, फट जाती हैं, पर त्वचा खुद नहीं फटती। खून बाहर रिसकर वहीं जमा हो जाता है। त्वचा के आर-पार यह एक गहरे धब्बे की तरह दिखता है।

रंग इसलिए बदलते हैं क्योंकि शरीर उस फँसे हुए खून को धीरे-धीरे तोड़कर बहा ले जाता है। खून को उसका लाल रंग [[haemoglobin|हीमोग्लोबिन]] से मिलता है। जब शरीर हीमोग्लोबिन को तोड़ता है, तो वह एक के बाद एक नए पदार्थों में बदलता जाता है, और हर पदार्थ का रंग अलग होता है: नीला-बैंगनी, फिर हरा, फिर पीला और भूरा। फिर निशान मिट जाता है।

sec.h: ताज़ा नील नीला क्यों दिखता है
sec.t:
बाहर फैला [[@blood|खून]] गहरा लाल होता है। पर त्वचा रोशनी के कुछ रंगों को बाकियों से बेहतर गुज़रने देती है। लाल रोशनी त्वचा में घुसकर बिखर जाती है, जबकि नीली रोशनी सतह के ज़्यादा पास से लौट आती है। इसलिए [[@skin|त्वचा]] के नीचे गहरे खून का धब्बा अक्सर नीला या बैंगनी दिखता है, जबकि खून असल में लाल है।

गहरे नील दिखने में एक दिन या उससे ज़्यादा ले सकते हैं, क्योंकि खून को सतह के पास फैलने में समय लगता है।

लोहे का कुछ हिस्सा हीमोसिडेरिन नाम के एक पदार्थ में जमा हो जाता है, जो सुनहरा-भूरा होता है। इससे पुराना नील कुछ समय तक भूरा-सा दिख सकता है, खासकर टाँगों पर। यह कुछ-कुछ [[@rust|ज़ंग]] के नारंगी-भूरे रंग जैसा है, क्योंकि दोनों लोहे से आते हैं।

नील के किनारे अक्सर बीच वाले हिस्से से पहले पीले पड़ते हैं, क्योंकि सफ़ाई बाहर से भीतर की ओर चलती है।

sec.h: कुछ लोगों को आसानी से नील क्यों पड़ता है
sec.t:
बच्चों की पिंडलियों और घुटनों पर अक्सर नील दिखते हैं। ये हिस्से फ़र्नीचर, खेल के सामान और झूले-फिसलपट्टियों से टकराते रहते हैं, और यहाँ त्वचा और हड्डी के बीच गद्दी बहुत कम होती है।

बुज़ुर्गों को आसानी से नील पड़ता है, क्योंकि उनकी त्वचा पतली और खून की नलियाँ नाज़ुक हो जाती हैं। खून को पतला करने वाली कुछ दवाएँ भी नील पड़ने की संभावना बढ़ा देती हैं। अगर किसी को बिना वजह जाने बहुत सारे नील पड़ते हों, तो डॉक्टर को बताना ठीक है।

हर नील बस त्वचा के ठीक नीचे नहीं होता। ज़ोर की ठोकर किसी [[@muscles|मांसपेशी]] में नील डाल सकती है, जिससे वह अकड़ जाती है और दुखती है, और भारी चोट से हड्डी तक में नील पड़ सकता है। ऐसे गहरे नील सतह पर शायद कभी न दिखें, पर डॉक्टर उन्हें स्कैन में देख सकते हैं।

अलग-अलग त्वचा पर नील अलग दिखते हैं। गहरी त्वचा पर ताज़ा नील नीला नहीं, बल्कि गहरा बैंगनी, भूरा या लगभग काला दिख सकता है, और हरे व पीले दौर पहचानना ज़्यादा मुश्किल हो सकता है। डॉक्टरों को सिखाया जाता है कि वे रंग के साथ सूजन और दबाने पर दर्द भी देखें।

sec.h: काली आँख और बर्फ़ की सिकाई
sec.t:
काली आँख बस आँख के आसपास पड़ा नील है। वहाँ की त्वचा पतली और ढीली होती है, इसलिए खून आसानी से फैल जाता है और रंग साफ़ दिखते हैं।

ताज़ा नील पर कपड़े में लपेटी ठंडी पट्टी या बर्फ़ कुछ मिनट रखने से खून की नलियाँ सिकुड़ सकती हैं और सूजन कम रहती है। इसके बाद इंतज़ार के सिवा ज़्यादा कुछ करने को नहीं होता। लगभग दो हफ़्तों में ज़्यादातर नील गायब हो जाते हैं, और उस खून का लोहा तब तक शायद नई लाल रक्त [[cell|कोशिकाओं]] के भीतर पहुँच चुका होता है।

text: Nobody can say for sure, but some changes are already starting. Many students may get an AI tutor that explains things step by step, at their own speed. Virtual reality could take a class inside a beating heart or onto the surface of Mars. Lessons may mix time in a classroom with time online.

Still, most experts think the school building and the teacher will remain at the centre. During the [[pandemic|pandemic]], children everywhere learned from home, and many of them missed their friends and teachers more than they expected. School is also where kids learn to work together, argue, share and make friends.

sec.h: The school you know is young
sec.t:
For most of history, there was no school as we know it. Children learned farming, crafts or trades from their families. Rich families hired tutors. In ancient India, students lived with a guru, and some travelled to great centres like [[@nalanda|Nalanda]], which had thousands of students and teachers.

Classes by age, with bells, desks in rows and a set timetable, spread from Prussia, part of today's Germany, in the 1800s. Countries copied the model to teach millions of children to read, write and do sums. Many of today's schools still look a lot like that.

In April 2020, COVID-19 closed schools for about 1.6 billion learners. Overnight, kitchens became classrooms. Children joined lessons on phones and laptops, if their families had them.

Many didn't. In India, lessons went out on TV channels and radio, and teachers in some villages taught small groups in the open air or over phone calls. The closures showed that technology can help, but also that it can leave behind children without internet or devices.

With [[@vr-ar|virtual reality]] headsets, a class in Lucknow could walk through ancient Rome or float inside the International Space Station. Some schools already use VR for science and history. A goggle-eyed field trip costs less than a real one, though headsets are still expensive and can give some people headaches.

Some scientists also think timetables may change. Research on sleep shows that teenagers' body clocks run later than adults', and some US school districts have pushed start times later so students can sleep more.

Augmented reality, which adds digital images on top of the real world through a screen, can make a textbook diagram of a volcano pop up and erupt on your desk.

India's National Education Policy of 2020 aims to change what happens in class. It wants less learning by heart and more projects, coding from the middle school years, and teaching in a child's home language in the early grades. A government platform called DIKSHA, launched in 2017, puts textbooks and lessons online in many Indian languages for free.

The hardest part of the future may not be the gadgets. It may be making sure every child, in a city flat or a remote village, gets a good teacher and a fair chance. As machines take over more tasks, the [[@future-jobs-ai|jobs]] waiting for today's students may need skills no textbook has yet been written about.

text: The Chalukyas of Badami were a [[dynasty|dynasty]] who ruled much of the Deccan from about 543 to 753 CE. Their capital was Vatapi, today's Badami in northern [[@karnataka|Karnataka]], set among red sandstone cliffs beside a lake.

They are remembered for two things. Their king Pulakeshin II stopped the great northern ruler Harsha from pushing south. And, near Badami, at Aihole and Pattadakal, their builders and sculptors experimented with temple designs, cutting caves and building stone shrines that helped shape Hindu temple [[architecture|architecture]] across India.

At Aihole and Pattadakal, the Chalukyas built in both styles, sometimes in the same complex. Builders experimented and borrowed ideas freely.

sec.t:
Around 543, a chief named Pulakeshin I built a fort at Vatapi and declared himself king. He chose well. Steep sandstone cliffs made Vatapi easy to defend, and a large tank of water lay at its heart.

His successors carved four cave temples into the cliff face. Three are Hindu, dedicated to Shiva and Vishnu, and one is Jain. Cave 3 carries an [[inscription|inscription]] dated 578 CE, made by King Mangalesha. Inside the caves are giant [[sculpture|sculptures]], including Vishnu seated on a serpent and an eighteen-armed Shiva dancing. The soft, even [[@rocks-types|sandstone]] let sculptors carve fine details that still look sharp today.

Pulakeshin II, who ruled from about 610 to 642, was the strongest Chalukya ruler. Harsha, who controlled much of northern India, marched south, but Pulakeshin defeated him near the Narmada river. The river became a frontier between north and south.

We know about this from a long Sanskrit poem carved on the Meguti temple at Aihole in 634 CE. It was written by Pulakeshin's court poet, Ravikirti, and it praises the king's victories. The Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang also passed through and described Pulakeshin's people as proud and warlike.

Aihole, about 35 kilometres from Badami, has more than a hundred temples from different periods. Some of the early ones look like village halls with flat roofs. The Durga temple has an unusual rounded end, a bit like the back of a Buddhist prayer hall. Historians often call Aihole a cradle of Indian temple building, because so many experiments happened in one place.

At Pattadakal, on the Malaprabha river, the experiments matured. Some temples have the curved northern tower called a *nagara* shikhara. Others have the stepped, pyramid-like southern tower called a *dravida* vimana. The grandest, the Virupaksha temple, was built around 740 by Queen Lokamahadevi to celebrate her husband's victories over the Pallavas. Pattadakal was named a [[@unesco-sites|World Heritage Site]] in 1987.

In 753, a Chalukya official named Dantidurga rebelled and founded the [[@rashtrakutas|Rashtrakuta]] dynasty, which went on to carve the [[@ellora-kailasa|Kailasa temple]] at Ellora. A later branch of the Chalukya family returned to power in the 10th century, ruling from Kalyani. The red cliffs of Badami, with their carved caves above the green tank, look much as they did when Pulakeshin's soldiers stood guard.

text: हाँ, लगभग पक्का। सिंधु की मुहरें, मनके और बाट मेसोपोटामिया के [[@sumer|उर]] और किश जैसे शहरों में मिले हैं, जो आज के इराक़ में हैं। मेसोपोटामिया की मिट्टी की तख़्तियाँ मेलुहा नाम के एक दूर देश से आने वाले जहाज़ों की बात करती हैं, जो इंद्रगोप, हाथीदाँत और बढ़िया लकड़ी लाते थे। ज़्यादातर इतिहासकार मानते हैं कि मेलुहा सिंधु का इलाका था।

यह व्यापार लगभग 2600 से 1900 ईसा पूर्व के बीच अपने चरम पर था। लगता है जहाज़ अरब सागर और फ़ारस की खाड़ी के तट से सटकर चलते थे, और मगन यानी आज के ओमान, और दिलमुन यानी आज के बहरीन में रुकते थे। उस ज़माने में यह दुनिया के सबसे लंबे व्यापारिक रिश्तों में से एक था।

sec.t:

यह छोटी-सी बात बहुत कुछ कहती है। मेलुहा के लोग इतनी बार आते थे, या शायद मेसोपोटामिया में बस भी गए थे, कि किसी ने उनके लिए अनुवाद करने को ही अपना पेशा बना लिया। मेसोपोटामिया के ताक़तवर राजा अक्काद के सरगोन ने शान से कहा था कि मेलुहा, मगन और दिलमुन के जहाज़ उसकी राजधानी के घाट पर लंगर डालते हैं।

sec.t:
सिंधु के व्यापारी पत्थर के घनाकार बाट इस्तेमाल करते थे, जो अक्सर धारियों वाले चर्ट पत्थर के बने होते। छोटे बाट हर बार दोगुने होते: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64। यही सेट सैकड़ों किलोमीटर दूर बसे शहरों में मिलता है, यानी हड़प्पा का व्यापारी और लोथल का व्यापारी सामान एक ही तरह से तौलते थे।

ईमानदार [[@weights-mass|बाट]] हर बाज़ार में ज़रूरी हैं, प्राचीन घाट से लेकर आज की सब्ज़ी मंडी तक। एक जैसे बाटों का सेट बताता है कि व्यापार सलीके से चलता था, शायद उसकी जाँच के लिए अफ़सर भी थे। सिंधु के लोग अपने बड़े बाटों के लिए [[decimal|दशमलव]] पद्धति भी इस्तेमाल करते थे, लगभग वैसे ही जैसे हम आज दहाई में गिनते हैं।

गुजरात के लोथल में पुरातत्वविदों को ईंटों का एक बड़ा कुंड मिला, लगभग 220 मीटर लंबा, यानी एक के पीछे एक रखी 11 क्रिकेट पिचों जितना। खुदाई करने वाले एस.आर. राव का कहना था कि यह एक नदी की धारा से जुड़ी गोदी थी, जहाँ नावों पर माल चढ़ाया और उतारा जाता था।

सब इससे सहमत नहीं हैं। कुछ विशेषज्ञ मानते हैं कि यह पानी जमा करने का [[reservoir|जलाशय]] था। जो भी हो, लोथल में मनके बनाने की कार्यशालाएँ थीं, एक गोदाम था, और फ़ारस की खाड़ी की एक मुहर मिली है, इसलिए यह साफ़ है कि यह दूर के व्यापार से जुड़ा था। समुद्र के पास होने से यह अपने-आप एक [[@sea-ports|बंदरगाह]] बन जाता था।

लगभग 1900 ईसा पूर्व के बाद मेसोपोटामिया के लेखों में मेलुहा का ज़िक्र कम होता जाता है। उसी समय सिंधु के बड़े शहर सिकुड़ रहे थे, शायद इसलिए कि नदियों ने रास्ता बदल लिया और [[@monsoon|मानसून]] की बारिश कमज़ोर पड़ गई। शहर ख़ाली होते गए, जहाज़ आने बंद हो गए, और मेलुहा की याद धीरे-धीरे लिखे हुए दस्तावेज़ों से मिट गई।

text: The Netherlands is a flat, low country on the North Sea, where several big rivers, including the Rhine, reach the sea. About a quarter of it lies below sea level, and much more would flood without protection. For centuries, the Dutch have built dykes, which are walls of earth, to keep the sea and rivers out, and dug canals to carry water away.

Canals do several jobs at once. They drain water from fields and streets. They act as roads for boats. In cities like Amsterdam, they also once carried goods right to merchants' front doors. Some canals are old rivers tamed and straightened. Others were dug by hand to turn swamps and lakes into dry land.

st.reveal: The houses are tall and narrow with very steep stairs. It is easier to tie a rope over the hook and pull a sofa up the front of the house, then swing it in through a big window. Some houses lean forward on purpose, so the load doesn't bang against the walls.

sec.t:
The Dutch have a saying: God created the world, but the Dutch created the Netherlands. Starting in the Middle Ages, they built a dyke around a marsh or a shallow lake, then pumped the water out. The dry land left behind is called a polder.

For centuries the pumping was done by windmills, which turned scoops or screws to lift water into canals at a higher level. Some windmills still stand in rows at Kinderdijk, near Rotterdam. Today electric pumps do the job, but the principle is the same. If the pumps stopped, large parts of the country would slowly fill with water.

Below Amsterdam lies wet peat and clay, too soft to hold up a heavy building. So builders drove long wooden posts, called piles, down through the mud until they reached a firmer layer of sand. As long as the wood stays under water, with no air, it does not rot. The Royal Palace on Dam Square rests on 13,659 of these piles.

Over time, some piles shift, and that is one reason old canal houses lean at odd angles. Many are also very narrow, with steep stairs, so furniture is hauled up the outside with a hook and rope.

On a stormy night in 1953, the North Sea broke through dykes in the south-west of the country. Around 1,800 people died. The Dutch responded with the Delta Works, a giant system of dams, barriers and gates finished over the following decades. Some of the gates stay open so tides can flow, and close only when a storm is coming.

With [[@sea-level-rise|sea level rise]], the Dutch are building higher dykes, but also making "room for the river": fields and parks that are allowed to flood safely. Meanwhile, the flat land is perfect for [[@cycling-tour|cycling]]. The Netherlands has more [[@bicycles-history|bicycles]] than people, and thousands are fished out of Amsterdam's canals every year.

text: The Great Lakes are five huge freshwater lakes in North America: Superior, Michigan, Huron, Erie and Ontario. The border between the USA and Canada runs through four of them. Lake Michigan is the only one entirely inside the USA.

Together they hold about 21 percent of all the fresh water sitting on the surface of the planet. Water flows from one lake to the next, from Superior down to Ontario, then out along the St Lawrence River to the Atlantic Ocean. Standing on the shore of Lake Superior, you cannot see the other side. The waves, beaches and lighthouses make it feel like the sea, until you taste the water and find no salt.

st.prompt: Lake Michigan and Lake Huron have different names on every map. What is odd about them?

One is fresh water and the other is salty

st.reveal: The Straits of Mackinac between them are about 8 km wide and quite deep. Water flows both ways, and the two lakes rise and fall together. Scientists often treat them as a single lake, which would then be the largest freshwater lake on Earth by area.

sec.t:
Lake Superior is the biggest by area of any freshwater lake, about 82,000 square kilometres, larger than the whole of Punjab. It is also the deepest and coldest of the five. Lake Erie is the shallowest, so it warms up fastest in summer and freezes over most easily in winter.

Between Erie and Ontario, the water drops over [[@niagara-falls|Niagara Falls]]. Ships can't go over a waterfall, so the Welland Canal next to it lifts and lowers them through a staircase of locks. Big cities line the shores: Chicago, Detroit, Cleveland, Milwaukee and Toronto. More than 30 million people in the two countries get their drinking water from the lakes, according to the US Environmental Protection Agency.

The lakes can be wild. In autumn, cold winds from Canada whip up waves taller than a two-storey house. On 10 November 1975, the cargo ship Edmund Fitzgerald sank in a storm on Lake Superior. All 29 crew were lost, and a famous folk song by Gordon Lightfoot still tells the story.

Thousands of [[@shipwrecks|shipwrecks]] lie on the lake beds. In cold fresh water there are no shipworms and little rot, so some wooden ships from the 1800s still have their masts standing.

In winter, the lakes make weather of their own. Icy air picks up moisture as it crosses the warmer open water, then dumps it as heavy "lake-effect" snow on cities such as Buffalo.

By the 1960s, factories and towns were pouring waste into the lakes. Lake Erie was so polluted that newspapers called it dead. In 1969 a river flowing into it, the Cuyahoga in Cleveland, caught fire because of the oil floating on it.

The fire shocked people. In 1972 the USA passed a major clean water law, and the USA and Canada signed an agreement to clean up the lakes together. The water became much cleaner, though new problems keep arriving. Zebra mussels, small striped shellfish from Europe, came in the [[ballast|ballast]] water of ships in the 1980s. These [[@invasive-species|invasive species]] now carpet rocks and pipes across the lakes, filtering out the tiny food that native fish need.

text: The Atal Tunnel runs for about 9 km under the Pir Panjal range of the Himalaya, near Manali in Himachal Pradesh. Before it opened, the road north crossed the Rohtang Pass, nearly 4,000 metres high. Snow and avalanches shut that road for about six months every year, cutting off the valleys of Lahaul.

To build the tunnel, crews drilled holes into the rock, packed them with explosives and blasted their way through, a few metres at a time. After each blast they sprayed concrete and fixed long steel bolts into the rock to stop the roof falling in.
It took about ten years. The tunnel opened on 3 October 2020 and is named after the former prime minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee.

st.prompt: Why did engineers dig the Atal Tunnel from both ends at once?

options.t: To finish faster, meeting in the middle
Because the rock was softer at each end
To let air in from both sides during digging

st.reveal: Crews worked from the south side near Manali and the north side in Lahaul. Snow often closed the northern end, so for many months most digging happened from the south. The two tunnels met in October 2017.

d.try: Dig a tunnel through a heap of damp sand from both sides, with a friend working from the other end. See how well you meet in the middle. Then try with dry sand, and notice why tunnel builders must hold up the roof as they go.
myth: Tunnels through mountains are simply drilled out by one giant machine.
Some tunnels use huge boring machines, but the Atal Tunnel was mostly dug by drilling holes, blasting rock with explosives and spraying concrete to support the walls, metre by metre.

sec.t:
The engineers used a method sometimes called the New Austrian Tunnelling Method. The idea is to let the rock help hold itself up. After each blast, workers cleared the broken stone. Then they sprayed a layer of concrete onto the fresh rock, and drove rock bolts deep into it, like giant nails pinning it together.

Instruments measured how the rock squeezed and moved. If it shifted too much, the crew added more support before going further. Later, a smooth concrete lining was added inside. You can see how other [[@tunnels|tunnels]] are built, from boring machines to underwater tubes.

Crews dug from the Manali side in the south and the Lahaul side in the north. Snow closed the northern end for months each winter, so most digging came from the south. On 15 October 2017, the two sides finally broke through to meet.

The [[@himalaya-form|Himalaya]] is a young mountain range, still being pushed up as India presses into Asia. Its rock is often cracked and crushed. About halfway through, the diggers hit a fault zone under a stream called Seri Nalla.

Here the rock was broken into rubble, and water gushed in. Mud and loose stone poured into the tunnel. A stretch of only about 600 metres took years to get through. Engineers had to drain the water, support the loose ground with steel and concrete, and creep forward slowly.

That one zone is a big reason the tunnel opened later than first planned.

{{story:roads-built}}

sec.h: A safe road under a mountain
sec.t:
The Atal Tunnel is horseshoe-shaped, with one tube carrying two lanes of traffic. Beneath the road runs a separate escape tunnel. If there is a fire or crash, people can go down to this hidden passage and walk out safely.

Inside there are CCTV cameras every 250 metres, emergency phones every 150 metres and fire hydrants every 60 metres. Big fans keep fresh air moving, so car fumes don't build up. Lights brighten gradually near the exits, so drivers' eyes can adjust to the glare of snow outside.

At about 3,000 metres up, the air holds less oxygen than at sea level, and [[@altitude|altitude]] affects people. Building here meant workers had to cope with cold, thin air and long winters.

The tunnel cuts the drive from Manali to Lahaul by about 46 km and saves up to four or five hours. Villages that were once snowed in for half the year can now reach hospitals, markets and schools in winter. The road continues on towards [[@ladakh|Ladakh]].

In 2022, the tunnel was certified by the World Book of Records as the longest highway tunnel above 10,000 feet. It is a favourite stop for tourists, who pause at each end for photos of the mountains.

And the strangest part? Even longer tunnels run under the Alps and the sea, including one in Switzerland that stretches for about 57 km, as you can read in [[@extreme-longest-tunnels|the world's longest tunnels]].

text: Names have meanings because almost all of them began as ordinary words. Parents chose words for qualities they hoped their child would have, for gods and heroes, for things in nature, or for the day the child was born. Over centuries, many names travelled far from their original language, and people forgot what they meant.

In India, many first names come from Sanskrit, Persian, Arabic or Tamil words. *Aditya* means sun, *Priya* means beloved and *Noor* means light. English names often hide old meanings too. *Peter* comes from a Greek word for rock, and *Sophia* means wisdom.

sec.t:
Family names, or surnames, came later than first names in many places. In England, they became fixed in families from about the 1300s, as villages grew and there were too many Johns to tell apart. People were named by their job, like Smith (a metal worker), Baker or Taylor, by a place, like Hill or Brook, or by their father, like Johnson or Wilson.

In India, surnames can come from a village, a family trade, a title, a clan or a community. Many Marathi and Konkani surnames end in *-kar*, which links a family to a place, so the Mangeshkar family traces its roots to Mangeshi in Goa. Some Indians use no surname at all.

Many families mark a child's naming with a ceremony. In Hindu families, the *namakarana* is often held about 11 or 12 days after birth, and some families choose a first letter linked to the child's birth star. In many Muslim families, a baby's name is announced at the *aqiqah*, often on the seventh day. Some Sikh families open the Guru Granth Sahib at random and choose a name beginning with the first letter of the hymn on that page.

In the USA, the government keeps records of baby names from birth registrations, so trends are easy to track. Liam and Olivia have topped the lists in recent years. Names that were popular around 1950, like Linda and Gary, are now rare for babies, though plenty of grandparents still carry them.

Names change as they travel. The Hebrew name *Yohanan*, "God is gracious", became John in English, Juan in Spanish, Ivan in Russian, Jean in French and Yahya in Arabic. One name, five languages, and most people who carry it never realise they share it. Some Indian names have travelled the other way: Maya, for example, is now a popular name for babies in the USA.

Places get renamed as well. In 1995, Bombay officially became [[@mumbai|Mumbai]], after the goddess Mumbadevi, and in 2014 Bangalore officially became [[@bengaluru|Bengaluru]]. Every name, of a city or a child, carries a small piece of history that people repeat every day without thinking about it.

text: Ruskin Bond is an Indian author who writes in English about the hills, small towns, trains and people of north India. He has written hundreds of short stories, essays and poems, and more than fifty books for children. Many Indian schoolchildren meet him in their textbooks.

His stories feel special because they are quiet and true to life. Nothing huge usually happens. A boy saves money for a bicycle. A girl is offered a trade for her blue umbrella. A tree outlives the people who planted it. Bond notices small things, writes simply, and lets readers feel them.

sec.h: A lonely boy in the hills
sec.t:
Bond was born in 1934 in Kasauli, a hill town in today's [[@himachal|Himachal Pradesh]]. His father worked as a tutor and later served in the Royal Air Force during the Second World War. His parents separated, and his father, whom he adored, died when Ruskin was ten. That loss runs quietly through many of his stories.

He went to boarding school in Shimla and spent holidays in Dehradun. Lonely and bookish, he read whatever he could find and began writing as a schoolboy.

Since the 1960s, Bond has lived in Landour, above the [[@india-wonder-hill-stations|hill station]] of Mussoorie in [[@uttarakhand|Uttarakhand]]. For decades he has lived with an adopted family in a small flat, writing by hand at a desk by the window. Visitors climb the steep road hoping to meet him, and on many Saturdays he signs books at a bookshop on the Mall Road.

His landscape is the lower [[@himalaya-peoples|Himalaya]]: pine and deodar forests, leopards, langurs, mist, and the first [[@monsoon|monsoon]] rains drumming on tin roofs. In The Night Train at Deoli, a young man passes a tiny station every summer on the [[@indian-railways|train]] and glimpses a girl selling baskets. He never gets off. The story is a few pages long, and readers remember it for years.

Bond writes in short sentences and avoids fancy words. That plain style is harder than it looks. Like [[@rk-narayan|R.K. Narayan]], he writes about ordinary Indian life without explaining it for outsiders.

Trees matter in his stories as much as people. In Our Trees Still Grow in Dehra, the book that won him the Sahitya Akademi Award in 1992, he remembers planting trees with his grandfather. Old [[@banyan|banyans]], cherry trees and [[@mango-tree|mango]] orchards keep turning up, often outliving the humans around them.

Several of Bond's stories have become films. Vishal Bhardwaj filmed The Blue Umbrella, about a village girl and a jealous shopkeeper. His story Susanna's Seven Husbands became the film 7 Khoon Maaf in 2011. Children have also enjoyed television versions of his [[@ghost-stories|ghost stories]], which are more cosy than scary.

He received the Padma Shri in 1999 and the Padma Bhushan in 2014. He kept writing into his nineties, and his birthday in May is celebrated by readers across India.

text: The longest word in major English dictionaries is pneumonoultramicroscopicsilicovolcanoconiosis. It has 45 letters and is meant to name a lung disease caused by breathing in fine volcanic dust. The funny part is that nobody really uses it. A puzzle-maker invented it in 1935 to be the longest word, and dictionaries recorded it because people kept talking about it.

The answer changes depending on your rules. Chemists can build names thousands of letters long. Place names can be longer than most dictionary words. And English, unlike [[@sanskrit|Sanskrit]] or German, doesn't usually glue many words together into one.

sec.h: A word built as a joke
sec.t:
In 1935, Everett M. Smith, president of the National Puzzlers' League in the US, made up the 45-letter word for a meeting. Newspapers picked it up. It was so long and so odd that people loved it, and dictionaries eventually added it.

It is built like a stack of blocks from Greek and [[@latin-roots|Latin roots]]. The pieces are *pneumono* (lungs), *ultra* (beyond), *microscopic* (very small), *silico* (silica, a mineral in sand), *volcano* and *coniosis* (a disease caused by dust). Doctors just say silicosis, which is a real illness among miners and stone cutters.

Some long words are real and everyday. Antidisestablishmentarianism, at 28 letters, comes from a 19th-century argument in Britain about whether the Church of England should stay the official church. Floccinaucinihilipilification, at 29 letters, means "deciding something is worthless". It began as a joke among students at Eton.

Shakespeare used one long word just once, in the play *Love's Labour's Lost*: honorificabilitudinitatibus, 27 letters, meaning roughly "the state of being able to receive honours". It's still the longest word in his works, and it alternates consonants and vowels almost all the way through.

Others are shorter but still hard: incomprehensibilities has 21 letters. Uncopyrightable, at 15, is one of the longest English words with no letter used twice.

sec.h: The word that takes hours to say
sec.t:
Scientists name chemicals by listing their parts. The largest known [[protein|protein]] in the human body, titin, helps your muscles stretch. Its full chemical name, listing every building block, runs to about 189,000 letters.

People have posted videos of themselves reading it aloud, and one took about three and a half hours. No dictionary includes it, because it's more of a formula than a word. Titin itself is built by instructions in your [[@dna|DNA]], the longest "word" of all, written in just four letters.

A hill in [[@new-zealand|New Zealand]] has an 85-letter name in the Māori language: Taumatawhakatangihangakoauauotamateaturipukakapikimaungahoronukupokaiwhenuakitanatahu. Roughly, it means "the summit where Tamatea, the man with the big knees, played his flute to his loved one". Locals simply call it Taumata.

In Wales, a village has a 58-letter name, Llanfairpwllgwyngyllgogerychwyrndrobwllllantysiliogogogoch. Its railway station sign is a popular spot for photos. The name means roughly "St Mary's church in the hollow of the white hazel, near a fierce whirlpool, and the church of St Tysilio by the red cave". It was stretched out in the 1860s, partly to attract tourists, and it worked.

Some languages make long words easily. Sanskrit can join many words into a single compound. One famous compound in an old Sanskrit poem runs for well over a hundred letters in Roman script. German glues nouns together too. A legal word about checking beef labels, 63 letters long, was removed from law in 2013.

Long words are fun, but good writers usually prefer short ones. They're easier to read and remember. And English still keeps inventing new ones, short and long, as people need them, which is how [[@words-made-up|made-up words]] sometimes end up in dictionaries.

sec.t:
पिज़्ज़ा को [[@tomatoes|टमाटर]] चाहिए था, जो 1500 के दशक में अमेरिकी महाद्वीपों से यूरोप पहुँचा। शुरू में इटली के लोग उस पर शक करते थे, पर 1700 के दशक तक नेपल्स के ग़रीब लोग ब्रेड पर टमाटर लगाने लगे थे।

मोज़रेला ने खिंचने वाली परत जोड़ी। यह एक नरम, सफ़ेद चीज़ है, जो नेपल्स के आसपास के कैम्पानिया इलाक़े में भैंस के दूध से बनती है। आज कई पिज़्ज़ेरिया गाय के दूध की मोज़रेला इस्तेमाल करते हैं, पर भैंस वाली मोज़रेला अब भी वहाँ की ख़ासियत है। पिज़्ज़ा लकड़ी से जलने वाले [[dome|गुंबद जैसे]] तंदूरों में सिकता था, जिनकी गर्मी 450°C से ऊपर पहुँच सकती थी।

एक मशहूर कहानी के मुताबिक़, 1889 में रफ़ाएले एस्पोसितो नाम के एक पिज़्ज़ा वाले ने इटली की रानी मार्गरीटा के लिए एक ख़ास पिज़्ज़ा बनाया, जो नेपल्स आई हुई थीं। उसने टमाटर, मोज़रेला और बेसिल डाले, यानी इटली के झंडे के लाल, सफ़ेद और हरे रंग, और पिज़्ज़ा का नाम रानी के नाम पर रख दिया।

इतिहासकारों को पक्का नहीं कि यह कहानी सच है। इन्हीं चीज़ों वाले पिज़्ज़ा का ज़िक्र नेपल्स में 1889 से पहले भी मिलता है। शुरुआत जो भी हो, पिज़्ज़ा मार्गरीटा क्लासिक बन गया। 2017 में यूनेस्को ने नेपल्स के पिज़्ज़ा बनाने वालों की कला को दुनिया की सांस्कृतिक [[@unesco-sites|धरोहर]] में शामिल किया, बाक़ी परंपराओं के साथ।

1800 के दशक के आख़िर और 1900 के दशक की शुरुआत में लाखों इतालवी लोग [[migration|अपना देश छोड़कर]] अमेरिका जा बसे, जिनमें बहुत-से दक्षिण इटली के थे। वे अपने साथ पिज़्ज़ा भी ले गए। न्यूयॉर्क का लोम्बार्डीज़, जिसे अक्सर अमेरिका का पहला लाइसेंस वाला पिज़्ज़ेरिया कहा जाता है, 1905 का है, हालाँकि कुछ खाद्य इतिहासकार इस दावे पर सवाल उठाते हैं।

कई दशकों तक पिज़्ज़ा ज़्यादातर [[@new-york|न्यूयॉर्क]] जैसे शहरों के इतालवी मोहल्लों में ही खाया जाता था। [[@world-war-two|दूसरे विश्व युद्ध]] के बाद, जिन अमेरिकी सैनिकों ने इटली में पिज़्ज़ा चखा था, वे घर लौटकर और माँगने लगे। पिज़्ज़ा की दुकानें पूरे देश में फैल गईं। [[@chicago|शिकागो]] अपने डीप-डिश पिज़्ज़ा के लिए मशहूर हुआ, जो एक ऊँचे बर्तन में सिकता है।

भारत में [[@fast-food-history|पिज़्ज़ा चेन]] 1996 में खुलीं, दिल्ली और बेंगलुरु से शुरुआत हुई। जल्दी ही उन्होंने भारतीय स्वाद के हिसाब से अपने नुस्ख़े बदल लिए। पनीर टिक्का, तंदूरी चिकन और तीखी सब्ज़ियों वाली टॉपिंग मेन्यू में आ गईं, और कई दुकानों में शाकाहारी पिज़्ज़ा के लिए अलग रसोई होती है।

कुछ भारतीय टॉपिंग देखकर नेपल्स के लोग हैरान रह जाएँ। पर पिज़्ज़ा जहाँ भी गया, बदलता ही रहा, और ख़ुद इटली के लोगों ने इसके सैकड़ों रूप बनाए, [[@rome-city|रोम]] के पतले, कुरकुरे पिज़्ज़ा से लेकर नेपल्स के तले हुए पिज़्ज़ा तक।

text: Soybeans are packed with two things the food industry loves: [[protein|protein]] and oil. A dry soybean is about 35 to 40% protein, more than most other beans, and about a fifth oil.

Crush a soybean and you get two products. The oil becomes cooking oil and goes into margarine, biscuits and snacks. The leftover meal, rich in protein, is fed to chickens, pigs, cattle and farmed fish. A small part of the crop becomes tofu, soy milk, soy sauce and the soya chunks many Indian families cook in curries.
Soy also hides in labels. Soy lecithin, which helps oil and water mix, is in many chocolates, breads and sauces.

sec.t:
Soybeans were first farmed in China, at least 3,000 years ago and perhaps much earlier. They spread to Korea, Japan and South-East Asia. Cooks there learned to turn the hard beans into soft foods by soaking, grinding and [[@fermentation|fermenting]] them. Soy sauce, miso from Japan and tempeh from Indonesia are all made with the help of [[microbe|microbes]].

Tofu is made a bit like paneer. Soybeans are soaked and ground with water to make soy milk, then something is added to curdle it, and the curds are pressed into blocks.

Soybeans reached Europe and North America in the 1700s, but for a long time they were grown mainly as animal feed and to improve the soil.

sec.h: A bean that feeds the soil

sec.t:
Today, Brazil grows the most soybeans, almost 170 million tonnes in the 2024–25 season, according to the USDA. The USA is second. Argentina is another big grower and a leading seller of soybean meal. Together they grow more than half the world's soybeans. China buys huge amounts, mostly to feed its pigs.

Growing so much soy needs land. In Brazil, soy farms have spread into the Cerrado grasslands and, in the past, onto land cleared from the edges of the [[@brazil-amazon|Amazon]] rainforest. Big buyers and the Brazilian government have tried to stop that, with mixed success.

Soybeans became a major crop in India only from the 1970s and 1980s. [[@madhya-pradesh|Madhya Pradesh]] and Maharashtra grow most of India's soybeans, more than four-fifths between them, and take turns at the top. Madhya Pradesh is often called the "Soya State". Rajasthan grows a lot too.

Farmers there sow soybeans with the [[monsoon|monsoon]] rains in June and July and harvest them in autumn. Most of the crop is crushed for oil. The meal is sold as animal feed, in India and abroad, and some is turned into soya chunks. Soya chunks, made from soy flour after the oil is taken out, became popular as a cheap, protein-rich food that soaks up curry like meat.

The American carmaker Henry Ford was keen on farm crops. He hoped they could replace metal and oil in factories. In 1941, he showed off a car with body panels made from a plastic said to contain soybeans and other plant fibres. The project stopped during the Second World War and never went into production.

Today, soy still turns up outside the kitchen, in some crayons, inks and foam for car seats. Not bad for a small, plain-looking bean.

text: For thousands of years, people cleaned their teeth with chew sticks. They chewed the end of a twig until it frayed into soft bristles, then rubbed it over their teeth. In India this is called datun, and it is often made from neem or babool twigs. In the Middle East and Africa, people use miswak twigs from a shrub called the toothbrush tree.

People also used powders made from crushed shells, ash, salt or charcoal, rubbed on with a finger or a cloth. The bristle toothbrush came later, first recorded in China, and spread worldwide only in the last few hundred years.

st.reveal: Chinese brush makers used stiff hairs from the necks of pigs, often from cold regions where the hair grew thicker. Pig-bristle toothbrushes were used in Europe too, until nylon replaced them in the 20th century.

sec.t:
Ancient Egyptians mixed tooth powders from ash, crushed eggshells and myrrh, among other things. Ancient Greek and Roman writers describe cleaning teeth with crushed bones and shells.

In India, people used powders of charcoal, salt and herbs. Some of these old powders were very rough and could scratch teeth. Modern toothpaste is gentler and contains fluoride, which makes tooth [[enamel|enamel]] stronger. Fluoride toothpaste became common in the second half of the 20th century.

Chinese brush makers were setting pig bristles into handles of bone or [[@bamboo|bamboo]] by the 1400s. Travellers carried the idea to Europe, where some people used [[@art-materials|brushes]] of horsehair or feathers instead.

In England, around 1780, a man named William Addis was in prison. The story goes that he saved a small bone from a meal, drilled tiny holes in it and tied bristles into them. After his release, he started a company making toothbrushes. It went on to sell them for well over a century.

Animal bristles were stiff but soaked up water and held on to germs. In 1938 an American company began selling toothbrushes with nylon bristles, a new [[@plastic-made|plastic]]. Nylon dried quickly and lasted longer.

During World War II, American soldiers were told to brush their teeth every day, and they brought the habit home. Today almost everyone uses a plastic toothbrush, which creates a problem of its own: billions are thrown away each year. Some people now choose bamboo handles to cut down on plastic.

Your mouth is home to many bacteria. They feed on sugar and [[starch|starch]] left on your teeth and make [[acid|acids]] that eat into enamel, creating holes called cavities.

Brushing sweeps away the sticky film of bacteria before it can do much harm. Dentists recommend brushing gently for about two minutes, twice a day, with a pea-sized amount of fluoride toothpaste. It takes only a few minutes a day, but it helps keep your [[@teeth|teeth]] for life.

Some old ideas are being looked at again. Researchers have tested neem and miswak extracts in mouthwashes and toothpastes, with mixed results. Electric toothbrushes now buzz thousands of times a minute. The tools keep changing, but the morning [[ritual|ritual]] of cleaning your teeth is one of the oldest habits people share.
